title: Transforming Software Development with Generative AI: Empirical Insights on Collaboration and Workflow
extended_summary:
This paper examines how generative AI tools, especially ChatGPT and GitHub Copilot, are changing software development work practices and team collaboration. The authors focus on questions such as what GenAI is used for, how people interact with it, and what effects it has on productivity, learning, and teamwork. The study is framed as an exploratory investigation because GenAI in this context was described as a new and under-studied phenomenon.

The intervention/approach studied is the use of GenAI systems in everyday software development tasks, including getting unstuck on problems, learning new topics, creating virtual environments, copywriting, generating boilerplate code, and working with existing code such as refactoring, debugging, and writing tests. The paper reports on semi-structured interviews with 13 professionals working in software-related roles, including developers, data scientists, managers, designers, and technical leaders, drawn from companies that had introduced GenAI into their product development processes.

The main conclusions are that GenAI often increases individual efficiency, lowers the barrier to asking for help, and supports faster learning and more enjoyable work. At the same time, the authors argue that frequent reliance on GenAI may reduce peer-to-peer communication and weaken the team learning loop, potentially harming collaboration and knowledge sharing in agile teams. They also note important challenges such as privacy concerns, lack of tool integration, outdated training data, and the need for careful prompt engineering to get useful output.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative exploratory multi-case interview study with 13 participants, which provides useful descriptive evidence but not causal identification. It is peer-reviewed and methodologically transparent, but it does not meet experimental or quasi-experimental credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests meaningful workflow and collaboration changes, but all evidence is self-reported and qualitative with no quantified effect sizes. Its impact is therefore plausible but unclear in magnitude, especially for education-related outcomes.

interventions.use_case: Use of ChatGPT as a conversational assistant for software development tasks, including rubber-duck debugging, code explanation, boilerplate generation, learning new topics, and prompt-engineered roleplay for coding and review support.

finding.finding_summary: Interviewees consistently reported that ChatGPT/GenAI reduced time spent on repetitive and manual tasks, improved speed of getting unstuck, and shortened writing or coding workflows. No numeric effect size was reported; the evidence is qualitative from n=13 participants across developer, manager, designer, and data science roles.
finding.measure: Interview-reported productivity, time savings, and workflow efficiency

finding.finding_summary: The paper reports that GenAI supported learning, problem solving, and prompting as a form of metacognitive support, but also reduced human-to-human collaboration and pair programming in some cases. Participants described faster learning and better thought structuring, alongside concerns about weaker knowledge sharing in teams.
finding.measure: Interview themes on learning, debugging, collaboration, and knowledge sharing

finding.finding_summary: Participants reported increased motivation, enjoyment, and work satisfaction when GenAI removed tedious work and made interactions feel more natural and less socially taxing than asking colleagues. The study is qualitative and does not report effect sizes; findings are based on n=13 interviews.
finding.measure: Interview-reported motivation, enjoyment, and work satisfaction

finding.finding_summary: The study argues that GenAI may reshape team structures and knowledge-sharing norms, potentially disrupting agile learning loops while also enabling new practices such as pair prompt engineering. Evidence is qualitative and exploratory, with no effect size reported; conclusions are drawn from n=13 interviews.
finding.measure: Interview themes on teamwork, knowledge sharing, and agile team dynamics
